hooks.text: Shine so brightly that astronomers study it in broad daylight.
A comet once shone so brightly it was studied in broad daylight.
In 1976, one comet reached a peak brightness of magnitude minus three.

title: The Comet That Outshone the Sun
description: In 1976, Comet West became so bright it was visible at high noon before the Sun’s gravity tore it apart.

beats.text: Shine so brightly that astronomers study it in broad daylight.
beats.visual: Telescope photograph of Comet West showing its bright head and tail, 1976

beats.text: On August tenth, 1975, astronomer Richard M. West discovered the icy visitor plunging toward the Sun.
beats.visual: European Southern Observatory La Silla Schmidt telescope, 1975

beats.text: In February 1976, the comet reached perihelion, racing within thirty million kilometers of the solar surface.
beats.visual: Diagram of a comet orbit showing perihelion and trajectory near the Sun

beats.text: Solar heat and forward scattering pushed its brightness to magnitude minus three, making it as bright as Venus.
beats.visual: Artist concept illustration of a long period comet nucleus approaching the Sun

beats.text: From February twenty-fifth to the twenty-seventh, observers tracked the dazzling object in the middle of the day.
beats.visual: Telescope image of Comet West seen in the bright daytime sky

beats.text: But the sun's gravity was a hammer, shattering the comet's nucleus into four distinct, glowing fragments.
beats.visual: Artist concept of a comet nucleus fracturing into multiple fragments

beats.text: This broken traveler will now spend hundreds of thousands of years drifting through the darkness of deep space.
beats.visual: Illustration of a comet trajectory moving away toward the Oort Cloud
